issues.legal_issue: Children born from a marriage void because it was contracted while an earlier spouse was living are legitimate and may be treated as successors to their parent’s property for the purposes of an eviction proceeding.
material_facts: The deceased owner contracted a second marriage while his first marriage was subsisting.
Two daughters were born from the second marriage.
The daughters were joined in the pending revision concerning an eviction proceeding over property owned by their father.
The court held that their inheritance rights did not require final adjudication in the eviction proceeding.
issues.conclusion: The daughters were entitled to be treated as successors to their father’s property for the purposes of the eviction proceeding, although their ultimate rights of inheritance and title were not finally determined.
issues.legal_principle: Section 5(i) of the Hindu Marriage Act, 1955 bars a marriage when either party has a living spouse, and section 11 makes a marriage in contravention of that condition void. Under section 16(1), a child of a marriage void under section 11 is legitimate and may succeed to a parent’s property. The court relied on these provisions while clarifying that the eviction proceeding did not finally determine title.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to evict a tenant from property under tenancy law.
predicates.deceased_parent_owned_disputed_property: The parent of the child owned the property in dispute and had died.
predicates.child_born_from_marriage_during_prior_ma: The child was born from a marriage contracted while an earlier marriage of that parent was still subsisting.

issues.definition: When a tenancy eviction proceeding concerns property owned by a deceased parent, a child born from a marriage contracted during that parent’s subsisting earlier marriage is treated as a successor for purposes of the proceeding.

issues.legal_issue: A tenant who was inducted into possession by a claimant and has not surrendered possession cannot deny that claimant’s title as a basis for resisting eviction, even if the claimant did not inherit the property.
material_facts: The claimant inducted the appellants into possession as tenants.
The appellants paid rent for a period and then stopped paying.
The appellants had not restored possession to the claimant by surrender.
The courts below found grounds of default and subletting, and those findings were not challenged before the Supreme Court.
The claimant was found not to have inherited the property from its deceased owner.
issues.conclusion: The claimant could maintain the eviction proceeding and obtain an eviction order despite not having inherited the property.
issues.legal_principle: Section 116 of the Evidence Act, 1872 prevents a tenant who has been let into possession from denying the landlord’s title while the tenancy continues and possession has not been surrendered. The court relied on Bilas Kunwar v. Desraj Ranjit Singh, Atyam Veerraju v. Pechetti Venkanna, and Tej Bhan Madan v. II Additional District Judge, and applied the rule despite the claimant’s lack of inherited title.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to evict a tenant from property under tenancy law.
predicates.claimant_inducted_tenant: The claimant placed the tenant in possession of the property as a tenant.
predicates.tenant_paid_rent_then_stopped: The tenant paid rent to the claimant for a period and later stopped paying it.

issues.definition: If a claimant inducted a tenant, rent was later stopped, possession was not surrendered, eviction grounds were found, and the claimant lacks inherited title, the claimant may still maintain eviction.

issues.legal_issue: An eviction proceeding based on the landlord-tenant relationship does not finally determine title to the property, which may be considered incidentally but must be left for comprehensive adjudication.
material_facts: The proceeding sought eviction of tenants on grounds including default and subletting.
The parties disputed whether the claimant and her daughters had inherited the property.
The court considered that the tenancy relationship and the grounds for eviction could be decided without finally determining the daughters’ title or inheritance rights.
issues.conclusion: The eviction proceeding could determine whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether eviction was warranted, but it did not finally determine title or inheritance rights.
issues.legal_principle: In an eviction proceeding, the court decides whether the landlord-tenant relationship exists; title may be considered incidentally but cannot be finally decided. A comprehensive suit for title is the appropriate proceeding for final determination of competing title and inheritance claims.

predicates.tenancy_eviction_proceeding: A proceeding was brought to evict a tenant from property under tenancy law.
predicates.competing_title_or_inheritance_claims: The parties disputed who held title to the property or inherited it.
predicates.eviction_decision_turns_on_tenancy_relat: The eviction question could be decided by determining whether a landlord-tenant relationship existed and whether eviction grounds were established.

issues.definition: When an eviction decision turns on the tenancy relationship despite competing title or inheritance claims, the proceeding does not finally determine title.
